$comment: Benchmark queries: same Cypher, two engines (Relate local .rl vs Neo4j Cloud).
Every query is written to run unmodified on both, so the only variable is the engine.
Params use $name syntax, identical in Relate and Neo4j drivers.
`tier` groups queries by shape: lookup, traversal, aggregate, vector.
A benchmark that only measures one tier will flatter whichever engine wins that tier.

queries.why: Indexed point lookup. The floor: both engines should be fast, so a bad result here means a missing index, not a slow engine.
Range scan on time within one thread. Tests whether ts_utc is indexed usefully.
queries.cypher: MATCH (m:Message)-[:IN]->(t:Thread {key: $thread}) WHERE m.ts_utc >= $since AND m.ts_utc < $until RETURN m.key, m.ts_utc ORDER BY m.ts_utc

queries.why: 1-2 hops over REPLY_TO. If Relate is a real graph engine this is where local wins hardest, because there is no network round trip per hop.
queries.cypher: MATCH (m:Message {key: $key})-[:REPLY_TO*1..3]->(r:Message) RETURN r.key, r.body ORDER BY r.ts_utc

queries.why: Person -> Message -> Thread, bounded by date. The query the UI's relation buttons will run.
queries.cypher: MATCH (p:Person)-[:SENT]->(m:Message)-[:IN]->(t:Thread) WHERE m.ts_utc >= $since RETURN p.display_name AS who, t.key AS thread, count(m) AS n ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT $limit

queries.why: Two people, shared threads. A join, which is where a graph engine should beat a relational plan.
Group-by over the whole store. This is usually where cloud wins, so including it keeps the comparison honest.
queries.cypher: MATCH (m:Message) RETURN m.platform AS platform, count(m) AS n ORDER BY n DESC

queries.why: Feeds the evidence panel: how many non-text rows were kept rather than dropped.
queries.cypher: MATCH (m:Message) WHERE m.raw_kind <> 'text' RETURN m.raw_kind AS kind, count(m) AS n ORDER BY n DESC

queries.why: Native in Relate (db.index.vector.queryNodes, verified 2026-11-14). Same call exists in Neo4j, so this measures index build + query, not API shape.
queries.cypher: CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes($index, $k, $embedding) YIELD node, score RETURN node.key AS key, score ORDER BY score DESC

queries.why: The interesting one: nearest 10 messages, then expand to their threads and senders. Pure Cypher, so it runs unchanged on both engines.
queries.cypher: CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes($index, $k, $embedding) YIELD node, score MATCH (node)-[:IN]->(t:Thread) OPTIONAL MATCH (p:Person)-[:SENT]->(node) RETURN node.key AS msg, score, t.key AS thread, p.display_name AS who ORDER BY score DESC

queries.why: Daily re-ingest cost. Relate is embedded, so the comparison is file I/O vs network; Neo4j Cloud will look slow here and that is a legitimate finding, not a trick.
queries.cypher: UNWIND $rows AS row MERGE (m:Message {key: row.key}) SET m.platform = row.platform, m.ts_utc = row.ts_utc, m.body = row.body RETURN count(m) AS written

method: Warm up with 3 runs, then measure 20. Report median and p95, not mean — one GC pause ruins a mean.
Run both engines on the same machine from the same process where possible, so client overhead is constant.
Record: query id, tier, engine, median_ms, p95_ms, rows_returned, store_size_bytes.
A result is only valid if rows_returned matches between engines. Different answers are a correctness bug, not a speed result.
Publish the .json output next to the README. 'Fast' without a reproducible artifact is a claim, not a finding.
